_about: The consequence ledger. One entry per choice; one line per field. Read with `python3 engine/saga.py now|due`; write with `saga.py add|fire|void`. Never rendered.

baseline.note: approval before any ledger entry; check verifies baseline + sum(now.approval) == world.json

entries.chose: Asked the Prior to have the lay brothers tell the valley the Faithless went down the far side a week ago; for the river dead, to keep more blood off the House

due.what: Open on the Prior answering the lie with a question, and the lie going down the Steps with the winch-brothers; he said it remembering the river and the men it kept, to spare the House a fight
Marrant has heard the valley story and climbs anyway; one line of his about reading to empty beds

entries.chose: Played Hollis at knucklebones for a story told true and won the stone: Hollis is two days dry, three by the dusk bell, and has now told the Captain

due.what: Hollis is dry and Darrow knows it; neither says so in front of Benedek, and Darrow does not ask Hollis how he is

entries.chose: Said the oath with Benedek at the hour bell, lips moving and no sound, for the lad's sake; nothing came, and Hollis saw

due.what: Benedek expects the Captain's mouth beside his at the bells now, and says so to nobody; Hollis has seen it and says nothing either

entries.chose: Stayed on the gate wall with Rae after Wren left: asked after her oxen (she would not give their names: "They know them"), got a line about Hollis out of her, and sat when she sat, because she had seen the leg shaking

due.what: Rae would not tell him her oxen's names ("They know them."); the day she tells him one unasked, it lands as a small gift, said once and not remarked on

entries.chose: Crossed the court to the bars in front of the whole House and answered to his name: called Marrant back from the head of the Steps by both names and gave his own and his rank; nobody went down the far side and nobody is going down this one

due.what: The Prior refuses the writ for a named man, not for a list: at Old Mercy, Marrant demands the Captain of the Ninth by name, and the House knows whose name it is keeping

The Lowmarch has heard that the captain of the Ninth stood up at the gate of Saint Ysolde and would not kneel: the Faithless take heart from it (apply faithless +5 in a Book II entry when the company reaches the valley)

Downstream of `named_himself` (b1.2): open what follows the way the arc's Downstream line for this choice says (`saga.py arc b1.2`); fire where it is honoured, void with a reason if the story made it moot

entries.chose: Went after Wren on the wall-walk instead of the hall; kept her count of the hall lamps while she told him how stupid giving his name was, and promised to tell her first next time he means to be brave

due.what: Darrow promised Wren he would tell her first the next time he means to be brave; she wrote the count of it in her ledger, at one. The day he does, or does not, she counts it

entries.chose: Went to the Prior in the chapel for the reproach she had not given him; she gave him questions instead, and told him she says the names of everyone under her roof every night, his among them

due.what: Mother Ione says the names of everyone under her roof every night in the chapel and notices which she has had to stop saying; the Captain is among them, and was before he gave his name at the gate. Fire it where a name has to come out of her count, or where he hears his in it
due.evidence: I say every name under this roof in this chapel every night, Captain, and I have not had to stop saying one since you came.

entries.chose: Went down the hall in the dark to his three Ninth men from the gate with an order (go on not knowing me; I'll tell the Confessor you're not mine); the oldest called it deciding for them without asking, one said he would take the Confessor's bargain if there were one, and Darrow let the order go and asked what they wanted: to be asked, next time, before

due.what: His three Ninth men from the gate (unnamed on the page) refused to be bought off the Confessor's paper by his kneeling ("We came up those Steps on other men's backs, Captain. We'll not go down them on yours"), and he promised them "You'll be asked" before he decides for them again. Honour it at the crossing: before he goes down the Steps he asks them, or decides for them and they say so; Wren holds a sister promise (c02.1a)

entries.chose: Carried the Ninth men's refusal straight to Hollis ("Would you have let me go down for you?"), and when Hollis would not answer, made him over knucklebones for a story told true; won the stone by a hair; Hollis confessed that at the window he had wanted it for a moment, and now would carry Darrow down the Steps himself before letting the Confessor have him; Darrow made him promise to say such things aloud next time

due.what: Hollis told the Captain, as a story told true over knucklebones, that at the window he had wanted for a moment that Darrow go down and kneel for the rest of the paper, and that now he would carry him down the Steps himself first; Darrow forgave it ("I know what a man can think in one") and made him swear to say the next such thought to his face ("Out loud. Bells help me"). Fire it where Hollis has to stand by him at a cost, where the kneeling is put to Darrow again in Hollis's hearing, or where Hollis keeps a thought to himself that he swore to say

entries.chose: Followed Maelis to the far cots and asked what the glass was; she withheld until he said the thing he had come to say: under the bell's law a man who cannot answer has no will to be taken against, so the Confessor can carry the lad down without breaking it. She gave him the slow way every time as an order, and sent him to make Garrow eat

due.what: Darrow has said aloud, to Maelis and nobody else, that a Hollowed man has no will the bell's law protects: the Confessor could take the lad down the Steps without breaking it. The next scene carries it as his private dread while the House looks for a hand to blame
Maelis's order at the far cots: the slow way, every time, or Wren counts his steps and reads her the number at every bell. Fire it where he hurries, or where Wren is seen counting them

entries.chose: Took half a feast loaf to Hollis, who would not eat for Maelis and would not let go of Benedek's hand; held the lad's hand himself for the length of the loaf so Hollis could eat with a hand that was never empty, and gave it back

due.what: Hollis ate the feast bread only because Darrow held Benedek's hand for him and filled his own with the loaf, so it never shook: "Tell her I ate. Don't tell her how." Darrow owes him that silence. Fire it where Maelis asks how, or where the hall sees Hollis's hands empty

entries.chose: Read the night novice (awake all night, watching the door) and outwaited the kitchen (the flour clean at dawn), held Wren to counting what did not happen, and told the hall from his cot that nobody passed: not a grey cloak, not a lay brother, not the Mender, before the Confessor's word could settle there

due.what: The hall heard the Captain's account first (both doors barred at night and dawn, the nine keys where they hang, the far-lamp novice awake all night, the kitchen flour clean: nobody passed) and turned back from the Mender; at the climax the House weighs Marrant's ember witchcraft against a word it already has, not the other way round

entries.chose: Found the kitchen's book taking odds on which cot is Hollowed next (Hollis at four, himself at five, the Grey Cot with no price because nothing is left there to take); did not shut it, and bet on NOBODY instead: if another cot goes grey before the thaw he scours the kitchen ovens; if none does, the kitchen rubs out every price and stops counting cots

due.what: The kitchen's book carries NOBODY at long odds, the Captain's chore against it: if another cot in the hall goes grey before the thaw he scours the ovens; if none does, every price is rubbed out and the kitchen stops counting cots. The lay brothers have begun to put wicks on nobody. Fire where the book is consulted, the odds move, or the thaw comes

entries.chose: Asked the night novice if he might sit the far lamp with her; told her the truth when she asked if it would come again ("I don't know"); taught her what a watch is when you can do nothing; let her sleep and kept the lamp himself, trimming it till his fingers were black

due.what: Darrow sat the far lamp after the night bell and kept it alone once the night novice slept; the next scene opens with him short of sleep and wick soot in the creases of his fingers, and nobody passed on his watch either

entries.chose: Went to the kitchen after the night bell and found Rae reading the book; did not stop her putting her own stake beside his on NOBODY (if a cot goes grey before the thaw she carries the kitchen a load up the Steps on her back, and comes up when she is owing); asked again who gave her the letter and took her answer: a carter says who a load is for, not whose hand it came out of; read it, then ask again

due.what: Rae told Darrow to read the letter, then ask her again whose hand it came out of, if he still wanted to. Fire where he asks her again, or chooses not to

The kitchen book now carries Thorne, a load, under the Captain on NOBODY: if a cot goes grey before the thaw she carries the kitchen a load up the Steps on her back, not the cage. Fire where the book is consulted, the odds move, a cot goes grey, or the thaw comes

entries.chose: Played name-the-load with Rae on the gate wall at first light before she went down, for the other ox name against an aye; named the first load salt, and it was wet linen; owes her one aye; watched her go down without counting and told Wren not to

due.what: Darrow owes Rae one aye, lost at name-the-load on the gate wall: she will want it some day and will know when she asks. Fire where she claims it; he gives it, or does not

entries.chose: Answered Hollis's invitation in the cloister after dark: heard him confess the kind lies he told the lad (nobody was taking anyone; they would be let kneel) and ask whether they sent him; would not give him the easy no, said what his own eyes had (nobody passed, the cold came anyway, not yet from where), promised to tell him if it was him, and did not ask about the wax

due.what: Hollis began to tell the Captain to get some sleep, the words he said to the lad before the lad was taken, stopped, and asked him to sit up a while instead. Fire where Hollis next tells anyone to get some sleep, or lies kindly in Darrow's hearing
due.evidence: "Go and get some sleep, sister," he said. "The door'll keep."

entries.chose: Went to Maelis in her cell after the night bell to collect the rest of what she knew of the black glass; she would not say, made him look and say what it looked like (a chip off a field-stone), did not say no, caught his warm wrist when his hand went to it, and asked him to keep it out of the hall, since it gives Marrant a better word than witchcraft; he agreed: not in the hall

due.what: Darrow agreed with Maelis, in her cell, not to say in the hall that the black glass looks like a chip off a field-stone (it would give Marrant a better word than witchcraft; it clears her only when she can prove it). Fire where he keeps that before the House, or breaks it

entries.chose: Showed Wren the seam at dusk; could not get down to it, so she found it on her knees by touch (every wall sweats, this one is cold) and counted it three cots to the Grey Cot; stopped her following it past the third cot while the hall could see; told her first that tomorrow, when the fires are banked, he means to find where it starts. She counted it: Times you have told me first, one

due.what: Darrow told Wren first, Friday at dusk, that he means to find where the seam starts tomorrow when the fires are banked; she found it cold to the touch and counted it to the third cot, and he stopped her going past it. Honour it where they go to the wall

entries.chose: Went to Rae in the kitchen after dark and asked her again whose hand the letter came out of: the grey cloak at the winch-house, who said the Captain of the Ninth twice and smiled; she carried it up inside her shirt rather than leave it in the cage overnight with him over it. Pressed her on the cold in her cart and was refused (one a night); thanked her for the wax
Asked Maelis to take him down the undercroft stair herself, on her terms: her count, a hand on Wren's shoulder, her right to say stop; and if she says no, he waits

due.what: The stair is taken on Maelis's terms (b1.3 shape 1): it costs him a day of asking; her first unforced yes comes later in the week, in her own words and not as a bargain; at the descent, her count, one hand on Wren's shoulder, Hollis's voice from the top telling him to look at the wall and not the floor; she comes down after them without a lamp. She may still say no, and then he waits
due.evidence: Tell the Prior I'll take you down

declined: Send Wren down with a lamp.
Ask Mother Ione for the key, and wait.

entries.chose: Went to the kitchen after the night bell; the book has gone even money on NOBODY since the hall heard nobody's hand; would not let the novice rub out the prices (the bet is no cot grey before the thaw, not who did it) and gave her nights to cross off instead; Rae claimed her aye: when he has been down the stair he will tell her what the cold does on the stone, plain, not as he would tell the House; he said aye

due.what: Darrow owes Rae her aye: when he has been down the stair he tells her what the cold does on the stone, plain, not as he would tell the House. Honour it on the gate wall the night the House keeps her (slot 5), before her crate
due.evidence: So he told her, plain, the way she had asked it, and not the way he would have told the House.

entries.chose: Sat up at the Grey Cot with Hollis for the first hour bell of the night; asked what Hollis says to the lad every night (the truth he did not tell him alive, one bell at a time); at the bell said the lad's oath aloud, the first words of it out of him since the river, for the lad and not the Crown; Hollis watched instead of turning to the wall, and divided the night's bells between them: the Captain the odd, Hollis the even, and the fourth his

due.what: Darrow and Hollis keep the lad's bells in turns at the Grey Cot: the Captain the odd bells, Hollis the even, and the fourth is Hollis's. Fire where a night bell passes with them in the hall, where the fourth bell is spoken of, or where Hollis is heard saying the oath
due.evidence: it was Hollis who said them, gruff and low, without missing one

entries.chose: Wrote back to Aldric as a brother, the night the letters came, knowing a Confessor would carry it: yes, he turned toward Tobin and the knee went, and he would turn again; but the warmth went out of him first, before the mare, the boy and the turn, and whoever told Aldric was not there; he will not kneel, because he would be kneeling to that order told backwards; he nearly burned the letters so that Aldric would come, he wants to see him that much, and wants to understand what he saw from the river, which only Aldric can tell him

due.what: Darrow's answer to Aldric, written the night the letters came (quote it, or its lines, in the next scene's opening clause; it goes down by the bars in Marrant's hand, read by two): Aldric, Yes. I turned. I planted on a stone and turned toward Tobin, and the knee went, and I would turn again. But tell them the order, since you are telling them things: the warmth went out of me first, halfway across, before the mare went down, before the boy, before I turned. I was there. Whoever told you was not. I will not kneel. Not for pride in the leg: because I would be kneeling to that order told backwards. I nearly burned this so that you would come. I want to see you that much. I want to understand what I saw from the river, and I cannot, and you are the only man who can tell me. D.
due.evidence: I will not kneel. Not for pride in the leg: because I would be kneeling to that order told backwards.

due.what: Downstream of `vane_answered` (b1.3): open what follows the way the arc's Downstream line for this choice says (`saga.py arc b1.3`); fire where it is honoured, void with a reason if the story made it moot
due.evidence: Not grey. That's all I can tell you, and I'm the one who's been holding it.

declined: Burn them, as he burned the first
Keep them, folded, under the mattress

entries.chose: Asked Hollis what became of the writ from the ford; Hollis has kept it and never looked at the seal (if he looks he will know whose, and have to be a man who knows); Darrow did not ask to see it, and said he would like to be there when Hollis looks; Hollis: Aye. Maybe

due.what: Hollis said Aye, maybe, when Darrow asked to be there when he looks at the seal on the writ from the ford. Fire where Hollis takes the writ out to look at last, honoured (Darrow beside him) or not (alone)

entries.chose: On the first step of the undercroft stair, stopped and turned Wren round to tell her plainly she has been good to him since the Steps, and that he has had her counting for him as if she were the House's ledger and she is not; she buried it in counts, he stopped her, and she went without a number; she said he is the only one in the House who asks what she counted, not what it means, and asked him to come back up; he said down and up, she can count both; she counted it: Times the Captain has said a decent thing on a stair, one, room under it

due.what: Wren asked the Captain to come back up the undercroft stair (she will not have him in the book going down and not up), and he told her she can count both, down and up. Honour it where he comes back up: her count of both
due.evidence: Down and up, both columns, same number. Technically that's a clean page.

due.what: Wren keeps a count: Times the Captain has said a decent thing on a stair, one, with room under it. Fire where he says another plain kind thing to her and she counts it, or where she reads the count back to him
due.evidence: "Technically this is a ramp," she said. "It doesn't count as a stair." A pause, three steps of it. "It can go in the room under the one."

entries.chose: Sent his name down with Rae at first light as surety for the grey mare: a captain's word against a Holloway dealer's debt

due.what: Rae carried the Captain's name down the Steps as surety for the grey mare. Fire where word comes back up from the Holloway: whether the dealer took a Faithless captain's word, and what it cost (the finding itself is a stage of the second thread, rae.tether)
due.evidence: He said a captain's word was worth the mare's keep till the thaw, and nothing past it, and he'd hold her that long on it.

declined: Word, through Rae, that the mare is wanted for the House's stables, in Mother Ione's name
Nothing. Leave her where she is

entries.chose: Told Hollis and the far cots' keepers first what is under the House, the black sliver in the wall under the row and the satchel it came up in, and the Prior only after: his own people before the House's law

due.what: Mother Ione hears what is under the House after Hollis and the far cots' keepers have. She said at the stair head he would tell her when he knew what it was; she says once, to his face, that she counted the nights between, and asks nothing more
due.evidence: I counted the nights between. Two.

due.what: Downstream of `hollis_told_shard` (b1.3): open what follows the way the arc's Downstream line for this choice says (`saga.py arc b1.3`); fire where it is honoured, void with a reason if the story made it moot
due.evidence: Brother. Tell the Captain what you told me at the third bell.

declined: Tell the Prior everything: the black thing in the wall, the painted hall, the satchel.
Tell no one yet, and watch the stair.

entries.chose: At the wicket before the dawn bell, asked Rae what she wants, not the House, her; took her two answers (the cart and the oxen free of the debt on them to her uncle at the Coldmere inn; to carry a thing up the mountain once and see it come down whole) without pressing for the hand she will not name; and when she asked why his name went down for the mare, said the mare's name, Thistle, for the first time since the river, and that she will not stand under somebody else's word

due.what: Rae has the mare's name from him, Thistle, said at the wicket at first light, and went down saying she would tell her. Fire where she brings word of the mare, brings the mare, or says the name back to him

entries.chose: At the undercroft door between the dawn bell and the hour bell, asked Sister Pell what the bell says at dusk; said it again plain to her face when she lost it in the bad light; let her refuse him her hands with Ask the bell; took the three bells, the Small and Old Mercy's crack from her, and the four lines of the dusk verse knocked out on the oak; said them back and stopped on the third; and owes her a dusk under the tower, in the court, saying them with the strokes where she can see his mouth from the window

due.what: Darrow owes Sister Pell a dusk: under the tower in the court, saying the four lines of the dusk verse with Old Mercy's strokes where she can see his mouth from the tower window; late on a line and she will know. Fire where he says them at a dusk ringing, where she says he was late on a line or not there, or where someone else says the lines with him
due.evidence: He stood where he had said he would, under the tower, in the court, with his face turned up to the window where he could not see her and she could see him.

entries.chose: Came up from the kennels with the bitten hand and let Anselm bind it; asked about Mirren's mark (an M with a loop in the valley, like a hook, so it would hold, hers since she was five) and why she is the brave one (at twelve she answered the herald at the bell when their father was cried for the mill's debt; Anselm, fourteen, apologised to the herald); promised nothing; Anselm thanked him for what he does not know yet

due.what: Darrow knows Mirren's mark: an M with a loop in the valley, like a hook, so it would hold; Anselm says she has put it on everything since she was five and under her name on every letter. Fire where a letter comes with it or without it, where Darrow names the mark, or where the mark is seen on a thing that is not a letter
due.evidence: "Then the next letter up comes without the hook in her M," Darrow said.

entries.chose: Went looking for the farrier who has never been bitten; stood in his light; was shown the half-ring of marks on his hand and told it was a burn; read the Ninth's brand, a gate, off the chalk board; caught Hollis's remade leather cup against his chest with the bitten hand and took it up to the hall as the farrier's runner: Hollis is to put it on, stand, take ten steps not nine, and say where it bites, and the word goes back to the farrier

due.what: Darrow carries the farrier's remade leather cup up to Hollis: he is to put it on, stand, take ten steps, not nine, and say where it bites; the word goes back to the farrier, not to Hollis. Honour it where Darrow reaches Hollis with the cup in his hands, or where Hollis takes his ten steps
due.evidence: Hollis took his ten steps at the noon bell, with the farrier's new cup strapped on and the whole row pretending not to count, and swore at seven of them.

entries.chose: Asked Hollis, Wren and Anselm in turn what each would do with the price and said he is thinking of the letters: Hollis would let the Confessor wait and shield the brother; Wren laid out how a letter down could work (one he'd write, read at the winch-house) and asked what if it is caught; Darrow said the next letter up would come without the hook in her M, with Anselm there to hear it; Hollis set his price (the brother has heard the cost, not the words: he reads every word and knows what each is for before it goes down); Anselm said he would write whatever he is given and sit where he can be seen; Maelis asked who signs it and ordered both hands to the dawn forms

due.what: Hollis's price on the letters road: Anselm has heard what a caught letter costs; before any letter goes down in his hand he reads every word and knows what each is for, not what he is told it is for. Fire where Darrow shows Anselm the whole letter and its purpose before it goes down, where he sends one with its purpose kept from him, or where Hollis asks whether he did
due.evidence: "Before a word goes on that," he said, "you'll have all of it. What it says, what it's for, and what I'm doing to you by asking. Hollis's price, and it's a fair one.

entries.chose: Use him: Anselm's next letter down carries what the Captain wants the Confessor to believe, in Anselm's own hand and with his consent; the Confessor's price, the almoner for two names, refused

due.what: The false letter's fate, by the week's tier (the arc's Downstream for the almoner's beat, option 3): believed, and the Confessor moves later and a man short; or caught, and the almoner is lost to the House. The climax's second entry sets the flag the arc names

declined: Expose him to the Prior and the House.
Shield him and say nothing of the satchel.

entries.chose: Sat down with Anselm by the brazier, not close, and gave him every word of the letter and what it was for before he wrote it: three things for the House (the Confessor waits; a rider to Calden, one fewer on the terrace; what Anselm is told next says what the Confessor fears) and one for the sister, the one he cares about: the letter asks where she is kept and one thing only she could answer, the only road that goes toward her, where the trade would send Anselm down and get her nothing. Told him plainly he has not stopped seeing the trowel in his hand, and that he gets every word because the other way is the clerk's. Named the risk on her and did not soften it. Let Anselm's own line stand: The loop still holds. Said yes to his vow to answer at the bell at Coldmere when it is over. Hollis watched and called it paid

due.what: Anselm's vow, with the Captain's yes: when the letter's work is done, caught or not, he goes down to the bell at Coldmere where his father was cried, and asks aloud on its steps what was done with his sister. Fire where he goes, where he is stopped from going, or where someone says he means to

entries.chose: Took the knucklebones off Hollis and played him for the Sixth's brand; lost at the threes, left-handed with both hands bad; chanted the loser's rhyme and paid a story told true, how he broke his nose on a well-windlass at fourteen looking at a girl; got the brand the way the Sixth tells the Second, and the song, and one true part: the Second gave it them; Ash took the fifth bone under the cot

due.what: Ash has Hollis's fifth knucklebone under the Captain's cot and is chewing it; Hollis let her keep it, the stone. The set is four until she gives it up. Fire where the bones come out again and are one short, where Ash brings the bone, or where Hollis says she has it
due.evidence: "Four bones in his set. I'll be writing that down."

entries.chose: Asked Wren for the line she wrote at the council and shut on her finger; played her counting game (three counts, one embellished) and caught Hollis's song counted twice; read the line, Times the Captain has asked me what I'd do: 1; told her the letters are her road and that she is the third to know, and asked her to be the one who puts the letter in the carter's hands; she wrote under it, Times he did it: 1

due.what: Wren is to be the one who puts the almoner's letter in the carter's hands when she comes up the Steps, at the Captain's asking. Fire where the letter goes to the carter by Wren's hand, or where someone else hands it over instead

rules.then: Finale option 1 (shatter the First Stone) is always offered
Finale option 2 (take the Stone) is written as a true temptation; otherwise it is offered flat
Finale option 3 (return the tithe) is offered
Maelis tells her own story before Book IV, never before Book II: the gate is regard and a Book crossed together, so a warm first month cannot spend a late reveal
Hollis survives his last stand in Book IV
The duelist defects in Book III instead of dying
Carry-forward from arc t1.low applies
Carry-forward from arc t1.high applies
Carry-forward from arc t2.low applies
Carry-forward from arc t2.high applies
Carry-forward from arc t3.low applies
Carry-forward from arc t3.high applies
Carry-forward from arc t4.low applies
Carry-forward from arc t4.high applies
Carry-forward from arc t5.low applies
Carry-forward from arc t5.high applies
Carry-forward from arc t6.low applies
Carry-forward from arc t6.high applies
An 'arrives a chapter early' effect fires at most once per Book, whichever source armed it
The epilogue's last image after the final kneel is the form they made: a vow with no knee bent (arc rae.tether stage 5, rae.road)
Rae drives home at the next transition (a cost on company, never a death); the Tether's scenes wait until she is back a Book later; the stages never fall
The Confessor's seized ledger comes whole into Wren's hands, Rae's doing (b3.4); otherwise the page is half burned
At the Stonewright ring Wren finishes the line for him openly and says she will tell him why when it is hers to tell (b2.5); otherwise she is caught at it
Hollis names the Seated Blade on the page before Old Mercy (q1.blade stage 3 runs before b1.5); otherwise he teaches it on the tower stair itself, in the fight

evidence.ch04:s6: "That's the Seated Blade, Captain. Fight from where you're put."

rules.then: Wren stays at the House when he goes down the Steps (a cost on company, never a death) and rejoins at the mill (b2.3)
Hollis hears the writ's truth sober and asks for the second letter to read Aldric's hand himself (b2.4); otherwise the drunk hearing is available in any tier
Rae tells him she carries for the Lantern Market before the river mill (q2.lantern; sets rae_market_told true by her choice); otherwise he finds the oilcloth under the salt
Ysra comes over at the Long Night (q3.needle arrives her); spared but not won, she goes back to Vane alive with his words
Wren tells him her mother's name herself before any ledger is found (b3.4): the reveal is hers, not the paper's
The clans ride west with him in the main road as well as the high (t3, b4.1)
Maelis lets Darrow teach the first forms himself in the yard (b4.2) and the host sees a Warden; otherwise she teaches and he watches
Maelis says Permitted for the turn before he asks (b5.3), in any road
The Second's carters have turned, and q5.second opens half won in the main road
The last chapter's count is Wren's, said aloud to him

the Spire's lower door opens to Rae's word (the Market's wick calls in six years on the north road); the Market's price falls on her debt, the cart and the oxen, and he pays it or lets her (rae.road, Book VI)
